title: Carry the Word
protagonist: Ruth Mae Carter, a teenage church helper and message runner in Montgomery, Alabama

passages.text: Your name is Ruth Mae Carter. You are sixteen. You live on Cleveland Avenue in Montgomery, Alabama, in the winter of 1955. You sweep the floor at the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church and run notes between the deacons. Every morning you ride the city bus to work. The driver makes you pay at the front, then step off and walk to the back door to get on again. The sign over the seats says COLORED. You sit behind it. You have done this your whole life. You hate it. You say nothing.

choices.text: Ride the bus quietly, like always.
Watch the white riders, and remember their faces.

passages.text: On December 1, 1955, you climb on bus number 2857. The seats fill up. A white man stands with no place to sit. The driver, James Blake, turns around. He tells four Black riders to give up their row. Three stand. One woman does not. She is small. She wears glasses and a dark coat. She keeps her hands folded in her lap. You know her face from the NAACP office. Her name is Rosa Parks.

choices.text: Watch what she does.

passages.text: The driver leans over her. 'Are you going to stand up?' he asks. 'No,' she says. Her voice is quiet but it does not shake. The bus goes silent. You hold your breath. Two policemen come. They take her by the arm and walk her off the bus. She does not fight. She does not cry. She just looks tired and sure at the same time. Mrs. Parks turns her head and her eyes pass over you. She gives you the smallest nod.

question.question: Why was Rosa Parks arrested on December 1, 1955?
choices: She refused to give up her bus seat to a white man in the segregated section
She was caught voting illegally in a city election
She refused to pay her bus fare at the front of the bus
She organized a march without a city permit
question.explanation: Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger under Montgomery's bus segregation laws, sparking the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

choices.text: Run to the church and tell the deacons.
Sit frozen until the bus moves on.

passages.text: You run all the way to Dexter Avenue Baptist Church. Your shoes slap the cold pavement. Inside, the deacons are already gathering. A woman named Jo Ann Robinson has heard. She runs the Women's Political Council. By night she is at a mimeograph machine, cranking out leaflets. The ink smells sharp. The papers say: Don't ride the bus Monday. You stack them in your arms, still wet.

choices.text: Carry the leaflets door to door all night.
Hand them off and go home to sleep.

passages.text: You carry leaflets through the cold dark of Montgomery. You knock on doors on Jackson Street and High Street. People take the papers in their nightclothes and read by candlelight. 'Monday,' you tell them. 'Nobody rides Monday.' Some are afraid. Some grip your hand. By morning the word has crossed the whole city. You stand at the bus stop and watch.

choices.text: Watch the empty buses roll past.

passages.text: Monday, December 5, 1955. The buses come down Cleveland Avenue. They are empty. Black riders walk instead. They share cars. They ride mules. They go on foot in the cold, miles to work. The boycott holds. That night a meeting fills the Holt Street Baptist Church. The crowd spills into the street. A young preacher stands to speak. He is twenty-six years old. His name is Martin Luther King Jr.

choices.text: Push inside to hear him.

passages.text: You squeeze through the packed pews at Holt Street Baptist Church. The air is hot with breath and bodies. Reverend King grips the pulpit. He is new in town, the pastor at your own church. His voice starts low and climbs. 'There comes a time,' he says, 'when people get tired.' The crowd roars. He tells them to protest, but never to hate. 'We must use the weapon of love,' he says. 'We must use the weapon of protest.' He warns them not to lie down and not to strike back. He calls it nonviolence. You feel the floor shake under stamping feet. You have never heard a man say a thing and a thousand people answer it at once.

question.question: What method of protest did Martin Luther King Jr. urge at the start of the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
choices: Nonviolent protest rooted in love rather than hatred or violence
Armed resistance against the city police
Paying higher fares to ride in protest
Quietly waiting for the courts to act with no public protest
question.explanation: King preached nonviolence and love as the movement's weapons, a philosophy that would define his leadership throughout the civil rights movement.

choices.text: Volunteer to keep running messages for the boycott.
Decide it is too dangerous and step back.

passages.text: You join the work. For months you carry messages between the churches and the carpool stations. The Montgomery Improvement Association runs hundreds of cars to get people to work. The police hand out tickets for nothing. They arrest King for speeding. White men shout from passing cars. You keep walking. The cold turns to spring, the spring to summer. Nobody gets back on the bus.

choices.text: Keep going when the threats get worse.
Wonder how long people can hold out.

passages.text: You tell the deacons you cannot run messages anymore. Your mother is afraid. You are afraid. But you still walk to work instead of riding. Months pass. You hear about the carpools, the arrests, the long walks, all from the edge of things. One night a sound rolls across the city like thunder. Someone has thrown a bomb.

choices.text: Go to see what was hit.

passages.text: On January 30, 1956, a bomb explodes on the porch of King's house on South Jackson Street. His wife Coretta and their baby are inside. They are not hurt. A crowd of Black men gathers, angry, some carrying guns. King comes out onto the broken porch. He raises his hands. 'We must love our white brothers,' he says. 'We must meet hate with love.' He sends the crowd home. No one fights. You stand in the smoke and the broken glass and you understand how hard his way is.

choices.text: Stay in the fight no matter what.
Feel your fear turn to something harder.

passages.text: The boycott lasts 381 days. People walk through winter and summer and winter again. Then the news comes: the Supreme Court has ruled. In the case Browder v. Gayle, the Court says bus segregation is against the law. On December 21, 1956, King and others climb onto a Montgomery bus and sit in the front. You sit near them. The seat feels strange and free. You are crying and you do not wipe your face.

choices.text: Believe the fight is won.
Sense the fight has only begun.

passages.text: The buses change, but Montgomery does not. White men still glare. Snipers fire at buses at night. A girl is beaten at a bus stop. You finish school and you cannot stop thinking about the movement. King helps start a new group, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The struggle is spreading past one city. In 1957 you read about nine students in Little Rock, Arkansas, walking into Central High School past a screaming mob.

choices.text: Decide to leave Montgomery and join the work.

passages.text: In 1960 you are twenty-one. You move north for a while to find work, and you land in Harlem, New York. The streets there carry a different sound. On corners, men in suits and bow ties hand out a paper called Muhammad Speaks. They talk about Black power and Black pride, not about loving the enemy. One speaker draws a huge crowd outside a store on 125th Street. His name is Malcolm X.

choices.text: Stop and listen to him.

passages.text: Malcolm X stands tall on the corner. He wears glasses and a sharp dark suit. His words are fast and hot. He speaks for the Nation of Islam. He says Black people should not beg white people for rights. He says they should defend themselves 'by any means necessary.' He says freedom should come by the ballot or the bullet. The crowd around you nods hard. It is the opposite of what King preaches. He looks straight at the young faces in the crowd, at you. 'You didn't land on Plymouth Rock,' he says. 'Plymouth Rock landed on you.'

question.question: How did Malcolm X's philosophy differ from Martin Luther King Jr.'s during this period?
choices: Malcolm X emphasized Black self-defense and self-reliance rather than nonviolence and integration
Malcolm X wanted Black Americans to give up the vote entirely
Malcolm X agreed completely with King's nonviolent approach
Malcolm X believed Black people should leave the United States immediately
question.explanation: Malcolm X, then with the Nation of Islam, preached Black pride, self-reliance, and self-defense 'by any means necessary,' contrasting with King's nonviolence and integration.

choices.text: Feel the pull of his anger.
Hold to King's way, even now.

passages.text: That night you cannot sleep. Two voices argue in your head. King says love. Malcolm says fight. You think of the bomb on King's porch. You think of the men with guns he sent home. You think of the girl beaten at the bus stop. You do not know which man is right. Maybe both are. Letters from home tell you the movement in the South is growing. Students are sitting at white lunch counters and refusing to leave.

choices.text: Go south to join the sit-ins.
Stay in Harlem and watch a while longer.

passages.text: You stay in Harlem through 1961. You read every paper you can find. You hear of the Freedom Riders, Black and white together, riding buses into the Deep South to test the law. In Anniston, Alabama, a mob burns one of their buses. In Birmingham, riders are beaten with pipes. The news photos turn your stomach. You cannot watch from far away anymore. You buy a ticket south.

choices.text: Go to Birmingham, Alabama.

passages.text: You travel south and find the students. They sit at whites-only lunch counters in Nashville and Greensboro. They wear their Sunday clothes. White men pour ketchup on their heads, burn them with cigarettes, drag them off the stools. The students do not hit back. They are trained in nonviolence. You sit with them. Your hands shake on the cold counter. A man spits on your collar. You stay in your seat. The next year the movement turns to Birmingham, Alabama, and you go too.

choices.text: Go to Birmingham, Alabama.

passages.text: Birmingham in 1963 is the hardest city in the South. People call it 'Bombingham.' The police chief is Bull Connor. King and the SCLC come to break segregation here. King is arrested and thrown in jail. From his cell he writes on scraps of paper and newspaper margins. It becomes the 'Letter from Birmingham Jail.' A deacon reads it aloud to a room of volunteers. You are in that room.

choices.text: Listen to every word.

passages.text: The deacon's voice fills the church. King writes to white preachers who told him to wait, to go slow. 'Wait,' King writes back, 'has almost always meant Never.' He writes that justice too long delayed is justice denied. He says a just person must break unjust laws and accept the punishment, openly, with love. You think of all the years you waited. You think of the COLORED sign on the bus. You will not wait anymore. Then the leaders call for children to march.

question.question: In his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail,' what did King argue about waiting for justice?
choices: That 'Wait' had almost always meant 'Never,' and justice delayed is justice denied
That Black Americans should wait patiently for white leaders to act
That marching should stop until the courts ruled again
That nonviolence should be abandoned in Birmingham
question.explanation: King argued that telling people to 'wait' for rights almost always meant 'never,' defending direct nonviolent action against unjust laws.

choices.text: Help lead the children's march.
Try to keep the youngest children home and safe.

passages.text: On May 2, 1963, the children march. Some are only six years old. They sing as they walk out of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church. Bull Connor's men are waiting. They turn fire hoses on the children. The water hits like a wall and rolls them down the street. Police dogs lunge and bite. You pull a small boy out of the gutter and shield him with your body. The water tears at your back. Cameras click. The whole country will see these pictures tomorrow.

choices.text: Carry the boy to safety and keep marching.
Hold him and scream at the police line.

passages.text: The pictures from Birmingham run in newspapers across the world. People who never cared before are sickened. President Kennedy says the events shame the nation. The pressure works. Birmingham agrees to take down its segregation signs. You are bruised and soaked and proud. The leaders speak of something bigger now. They will march on the nation's capital. They will go to Washington.

choices.text: Travel to Washington, D.C.

passages.text: On August 28, 1963, you ride a bus to Washington, D.C. More than two hundred thousand people come. Black and white, old and young, they fill the ground from the Washington Monument to the Lincoln Memorial. People hold signs for jobs and freedom. A man helps run the whole thing from a clipboard. His name is Bayard Rustin. You help hand out water and box lunches in the heat. Then the singer Mahalia Jackson sings, and King steps to the microphone.

choices.text: Move closer to hear King speak.

passages.text: King reads from his notes about freedom and broken promises. Then Mahalia Jackson calls out, 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' He pushes his papers aside. He looks up at the sea of faces. 'I have a dream,' he says, 'that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.' The crowd answers like one great voice. You think of the bus, the bomb, the fire hoses, all of it. You are weeping in the August sun. This is the largest crowd you have ever stood in, and it is calm and full of hope.

question.question: What did Martin Luther King Jr. say he dreamed of in his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the March on Washington?
choices: That his children would be judged by the content of their character, not the color of their skin
That Black Americans would leave the South for the North
That the federal government would pay reparations immediately
That all protest would end forever that day
question.explanation: King's most famous line dreamed of a nation where his children would be judged by their character, not their skin color, delivered at the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

choices.text: Carry this hope back south with you.
Wonder if words alone can change anything.

passages.text: The march fills you with hope. But hope is fragile. Eighteen days later, on September 15, 1963, a bomb explodes at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham. The same church where the children began their march. Four girls are killed in the blast. Their names are Addie Mae, Cynthia, Carole, and Carol. You knew that church. You stood in it. The news guts you. You sit on your floor and cannot move for a long time.

choices.text: Let the grief turn you toward Malcolm's anger.
Cling harder to King's nonviolence.

passages.text: Back in New York in 1964, you go to hear Malcolm X again. But he is changed. He has broken with the Nation of Islam. He has made a journey to Mecca and seen Muslims of every color pray side by side. His anger has softened into something wider. He still believes in Black dignity and self-defense. But now he says he can work with others for human rights. He speaks of the ballot and of unity across races. He gives you his hand after the talk. His grip is firm and his eyes are calm.

question.question: How did Malcolm X's views change after his 1964 pilgrimage to Mecca?
choices: He moved toward the possibility of working across racial lines for human rights
He decided to fully adopt King's exact philosophy and methods
He gave up activism completely
He rejoined the Nation of Islam with stronger separatist views
question.explanation: After his pilgrimage to Mecca, Malcolm X broke with the Nation of Islam and became more open to cooperation across racial lines while still championing Black dignity and self-defense.

choices.text: Thank him and carry his words with you.
Stay torn between his road and King's.

passages.text: On February 21, 1965, Malcolm X is shot and killed as he speaks at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem. You are not there, but a friend is. She comes to you white-faced and shaking. Just like that, one of the movement's two great voices is gone, only thirty-nine years old. You grieve a man you barely knew but always heard. The struggle does not stop for grief. In Alabama, marchers are gathering in a town called Selma to fight for the vote.

choices.text: Go to Selma, Alabama.

passages.text: You reach Selma in March 1965. Black people here are kept from voting by every trick there is. King and a young leader named John Lewis plan to march from Selma to Montgomery, fifty miles, to demand the vote. On March 7 you walk with hundreds toward the Edmund Pettus Bridge. State troopers wait on the far side in gas masks, holding clubs. You climb the arch of the bridge and see them below.

choices.text: Keep marching down toward the troopers.

passages.text: The troopers charge. They call it later 'Bloody Sunday.' Tear gas fills the air and burns your eyes shut. Clubs crack down. You see John Lewis fall, his skull split open. Horses trample the fallen. You crawl off the bridge, coughing, dragging a woman beside you. Across the country, people watch it live on television. The whole nation sees what Selma does to people who only want to vote.

choices.text: Stay and march again, no matter the danger.
Help the wounded and decide whether you can go on.

passages.text: The horror on television changes things. Thousands more come to Selma from all over America. On March 21, protected by federal troops, the marchers finally walk the full road to Montgomery, your old home. King leads them up to the capitol steps where the boycott began ten years before. That summer, President Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act of 1965. It strikes down the tricks that kept Black people from the ballot. You stand on Cleveland Avenue again, where you first watched Rosa Parks, and you can hardly believe how far the road has run.

choices.text: Look back on everything you have seen.

passages.text: You sit on your old front step in Montgomery. You think of all of it. Rosa Parks, quiet and unmoved on bus 2857. King at Holt Street, at the broken porch, at the Lincoln Memorial saying 'I have a dream.' Malcolm X on the Harlem corner, then changed after Mecca, then gone. The children under the fire hoses. The four girls in the church. John Lewis falling on the bridge. The empty buses and the long walks. You carried messages, you carried a boy, you carried words across a whole country. Now you must decide what you will carry for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Carry the whole movement forward, scarred but unbroken.
Lay the burden down and try to forget the pain.
Let the grief of the dead swallow your hope.

passages.text: You become a teacher. In your classroom in Montgomery you tell children the true story, all of it, the love and the blood. You tell them Rosa Parks sat down so they could stand up. You tell them King dreamed and Malcolm warned and both were killed for it. You tell them about the bridge and the bombs and the long walks. Your hands still ache when it rains, where the fire hose hit you. But you stand straight. You carried the word across years and miles, and now you hand it to the young. The struggle is not over. You raise children who will carry it next.

You leave it all behind. You find a quiet job in a quiet town and you do not talk about the movement. When people ask if you were there, you say only a little. The marching, the gas, the dead girls, you fold it all away in a drawer you never open. The laws change around you and your life goes on, plain and safe. Sometimes a bus passes and your chest tightens. You look away. You survived, and you chose to forget. The years close over the memory like still water.

The grief is too heavy. You see the four girls every time you close your eyes. You hear the fire hoses, the troopers' horses, the shot in the Audubon Ballroom. The laws changed, but the people you loved are still dead, and no law brings them back. You stop going to church. You stop reading the news. You live, but something in you was burned out on that bridge and never came back. When children ask you about those days, you cannot make the words come. You carry the dead, and they are heavy, and you carry them alone.

finalQuiz.title: Final Check for Understanding
finalQuiz.instructions: You have traveled the historical arc and met key figures. Review the questions from your encounters and the standards this story was meant to teach. Then answer these questions.

questions.context: From your witness of Rosa Parks on the bus.
questions.question: What did Rosa Parks' refusal to give up her bus seat directly cause?
choices: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
The March on Washington
The Voting Rights Act
The Freedom Rides
questions.explanation: Rosa Parks' arrest on December 1, 1955, sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which lasted 381 days.

questions.context: From King's speech at Holt Street Baptist Church.
questions.question: What philosophy guided Martin Luther King Jr.'s leadership of the movement?
choices: Nonviolent protest grounded in love
Armed revolution
Total separation from white society
Avoiding all public protest
questions.explanation: King consistently preached nonviolence and love, even after his own home was bombed.

questions.context: From the long Montgomery Bus Boycott.
questions.question: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott finally end in victory?
choices: The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional in Browder v. Gayle
The bus company ran out of money and closed
The mayor personally apologized
Congress passed a law about buses
questions.explanation: The 381-day boycott ended after the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v. Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

questions.context: From your encounter with Malcolm X in Harlem.
questions.question: Which idea best describes Malcolm X's early message with the Nation of Islam?
choices: Black pride and self-defense by any means necessary
Complete agreement with King's nonviolence
Giving up the right to vote
Ending all forms of protest
questions.explanation: Malcolm X preached Black dignity, self-reliance, and self-defense, offering a sharper contrast to King's nonviolent integration.

questions.question: What did King mean when he wrote that 'Wait' almost always meant 'Never'?
choices: That delaying justice for Black Americans was a way of denying it forever
That people should never protest
That marches should always be postponed
That waiting in line was unfair
questions.explanation: King argued that calls to 'wait' were used to deny rights indefinitely, justifying direct nonviolent action.

questions.context: From the children's march in Birmingham.
questions.question: Why did the images from Birmingham in 1963 matter so much to the movement?
choices: They showed the nation police using fire hoses and dogs on peaceful children, shifting public opinion
They proved the marchers were violent
They convinced people segregation was harmless
They ended the movement
questions.explanation: Televised images of fire hoses and police dogs attacking children shocked the nation and increased support for civil rights.

questions.question: What was the purpose of the 1963 March on Washington?
choices: To demand jobs and freedom for Black Americans
To protest the end of the Civil War
To support bus segregation
To oppose the Voting Rights Act
questions.explanation: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom drew over 200,000 people and featured King's 'I Have a Dream' speech.

questions.context: From Malcolm X's return from Mecca.
questions.question: What change did Malcolm X undergo near the end of his life?
choices: He became more open to working across racial lines after his pilgrimage to Mecca
He stopped believing in Black dignity
He joined the Ku Klux Klan
He became a pacifist exactly like King
questions.explanation: After breaking with the Nation of Islam and traveling to Mecca, Malcolm X broadened his views before his assassination in 1965.

questions.question: What major law resulted from the Selma marches of 1965?
choices: The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The Montgomery Bus Boycott
The Emancipation Proclamation
The Letter from Birmingham Jail
questions.explanation: Public outrage over the Selma marches helped pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965, protecting Black Americans' right to vote.

questions.context: Looking back across the whole movement.
questions.question: What did the civil rights movement, led by figures like King, Parks, and Malcolm X, ultimately struggle to achieve?
choices: Equality and full civil rights for Black Americans
The right to ride buses only at night
A return to segregation
The removal of all laws
questions.explanation: The civil rights movement fought to end segregation and secure equality and full rights for Black Americans through both nonviolent and self-determination approaches.
